This is a Shiny app that I made to go along with a [paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-10642-x) 
that we wrote in the [Busch lab](https://www.buschlab.org) as part of the [Deciphering the Mechanisms of Developmental Disorders](https://www.sanger.ac.uk/collaboration/deciphering-mechanisms-developmental-disorders-dmdd/) 
project.
You can try it out on [shinyapps.io](https://richysix.shinyapps.io/baseline_compare/). The [code](https://github.com/richysix/baselineCompare) is on github.

DMDD was a project to study embryonic-lethal mouse gene lines, to identify 
critical genes for embryo development and survival. Our part of the project was 
to analyse the RNA-seq data produced for each mutant line. One problem was that 
a significant portion of the lines were affected by developmental delay, which 
is a common issue. In these cases, the homozygous mutants appear much young 
than the wild-type and heterozygous siblings from the same litter (as assessed 
by somite number). This makes it difficult to determine whether genes are 
differentially expressed because of the effect of the mutation or because of 
the delay. We developed a procedure to try and mitigate this problem using a 
large RNA-seq dataset of wild-type embryos, covering the span of the ages of 
the embryos in the mutant lines.

To allow other people to use this baseline dataset to analyse their own mutant 
line RNA-seq data, I created a Shiny app. 

The app accepts RNA-seq count data as two files, a count file and a sample file.
The count file needs a columns for the gene identifiers and a column for the 
count data for each sample. The samples file contains metadata about each 
sample.
The right-hand sidebar panel allows you to set various parameters and to start the analysis. There is a progress panel which prints the output from DESeq2 as the analysis can take some time.

![](deseq2-progress.png){fig-alt="Screenshot of the Baseline Compare Shiny app. It's a page with several tabs. The one shown has a right-hand sidebar with various inputs and radio buttons. The left-hand side shows the output from running DESeq2 in a panel labelled 'Progress'"}

The first thing it does is run a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with the 
input data plus the baseline samples. This allows the user to check whether 
their data is compatible with the baseline. If the wild-type samples in the 
experimental data cluster significantly away from the baseline then this is 
analysis is not appropriate.

The ***PCA*** tab shows two plots. The first shows the experimental samples and **only** the baseline samples with matching somite stages. The second includes **all** the baseline samples

![](pca-1.png){fig.alt="A screenshot showing the PCA tab. The PCA plot is an x-y scatterplot and shows that the wild-type samples cluster with the appropriately staged-matched baseline samples"}

It then runs differential expression analysis using the `DESeq2` package with three 
different sets of samples and model.

|Analysis Set|Samples|DESeq2 model|
|------------|-------|------------|
|Experiment Only|Experimental Data only| counts ~ (sex +) condition|
|Experiment + Baseline|Experimental Data and stage-matched Baseline samples| counts ~ (sex +) condition|
|Experiment + Baseline with Stage|Experimental Data and stage-matched Baseline samples| counts ~ (sex +) stage + condition|


![DESeq2 analysis sets](deseq-samples-models.png "Diagram of different analysis sets"){fig-alt="A Venn diagram showing the sample sets and model formulae for the three analysis sets."}

The differentially expressed (DE) genes are overlapped and specific subsets are assigned to 4 different categories of response as shown below.

![DESeq2 results sets](deseq-results-sets.png "Diagram of DESeq2 overlaps"){fig-alt="Four Venn diagrams showing how the results sets are made up. Mutant Response is the intersection of Experiment + Baseline and Experiment + Baseline with Stage. Delay is those genes in both Experiment Only and Experiment + Baseline, but not in Experiment + Baseline with Stage. No Delay is genes in Experiment + Baseline with Stage and not in the other two. Discard is genes in either Experiment Only OR Experiment + Baseline, but NOT both and also not in Experiment + Baseline with Stage"}

The ***Results*** tab has buttons for each of the four results sets. Clicking the buttons shows a table of the DE genes for that set sorted by adjusted p value.

![](results.png){fig-alt="A screenshot of the Results tab. The main content is a DataTables table with each row being a different gene and containing columns such as Ensembl gene id, Gene name, log 2 fold change and adjusted p value"}

If you click on a row in the results table it takes you to the ***Count Plot*** tab which has an x-y scatter plot of the Normalised Counts for that gene in the experimental samples and the matching baseline samples. There is also a button to download a copy of the plot.

![](counts-neurl1a.png){fig-alt="An x-y scatterplot with samples on the x-axis and normalised counts on the y-axis. The points are coloured by somite stage and show that the homozygous mutant samples have lower expression of the Neurl1a gene than the wild-type samples, which are similar in level to all the baseline samples"}
